title: Security projects: how do you get a control to everyone, and into IT projects before go-live?
short: Set a coverage target and dated exceptions before the pilot, run report-only first, and check every IT project at kickoff and before go-live.
answer: Before your next security rollout starts, write down its scope, a coverage target such as 98% of in-scope accounts enforced, and an end date for every exception, then run it in report-only or audit mode, a pilot and two or three rings. In the company's other IT projects, ask the security questions at kickoff and sign off before go-live, and scale the effort by protection need so only high-need projects wait for a full review.
audience: Heads of security, IT leads who own security, and project managers in small and mid-size companies

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Define done in numbers before you start.
items.text: Count the scope from the inventory and set a target, such as 98% of in-scope devices in block mode by 31 March, with an exception cap and an owner for afterwards. Count enforced, not deployed.

items.title: Watch before you enforce.
items.text: Keep each new Conditional Access policy in report-only mode for at least a week[^caplan]; it logs what it would do and blocks nothing[^careport]. Audit ASR rules first, except the standard protection rules[^asrplan].

items.title: Roll out in rings your help desk can absorb.
items.text: Pilot with IT and a champion per business unit, then a representative ring, then everyone. Microsoft advises waves within your support capacity[^mfaplan]; IT's own devices aren't representative[^rings].

items.title: Give every exception an end date.
items.text: Exclusion lists start short and grow[^caexcl]. Keep one exclusion group per policy, with a reason, an owner and an end date for each member.

items.title: Ask security at kickoff, not the week before go-live.
items.text: The BSI requires involving the ISB early in all larger projects and new applications and IT systems[^isms1]. Grundschutz++ lets you define when, so not every project needs it[^std3001].

blocks.title: Roll out a security change in this order

items.title: Who and what is in scope?
items.text: Count users, devices or apps from the inventory, not from the new tool; Defender's device discovery lists devices not yet onboarded[^discovery]. Which rollout comes first is the security program sheet's job.

items.title: What would break?
items.text: Run report-only or audit mode for one to four weeks and review the results with app owners. For segmentation, allow and log first, as the network segmentation sheet describes.

items.title: Who pilots it?
items.text: IT plus a champion per business unit, with a channel to report problems[^asrplan]. Turn what they hit into the user message and the help desk script.

items.title: When does the next ring start?
items.text: After a week with no open tickets in the last one. Reuse your Windows update rings if you have them[^asrplan].

items.title: Is it finished?
items.text: When the tail is closed by name, the old path is gone, such as SMS codes or the old agent, and an owner gets a monthly coverage report.

blocks.title: Users, help desk and rollback
items: **Tell users what changes, when, and how to get help**[^caplan], a week before their ring and on the day. Microsoft publishes templates for MFA[^mfaplan].
**Brief the help desk before each ring.** Give it the script, known errors and what to collect: user, time, app and the correlation ID from **More details**[^caplan].

**Write the rollback before you enforce.** Name the trigger and the switch: disable the policy or exclude a group in Conditional Access[^caplan], add an ASR exclusion rather than return the rule to audit[^asrtest], pause the Intune deployment[^intune].
**Exclude Mac, iOS and Android from report-only compliance policies,** or those users may get certificate prompts[^careport].
**In Germany, ask the works council early** about EDR, DLP and logging. It co-determines systems designed to monitor behavior or performance[^betrvg].

blocks.title: Exceptions that end
items: **Exclude groups, not people.** One assigned Entra group per policy shows who is excluded; the policy doesn't protect them[^caexcl].
**Record why, what instead and until when.** Each member gets a reason, a compensating control, an owner and an end date. Approval levels and maximum terms are in the risk register sheet.
**Let reviews remove people.** Entra access reviews can ask members weekly whether they still need it and remove those who don't answer. They need Entra ID P2 or ID Governance[^caexcl].
**Cap them.** Our rule: at most 2% of the scope at go-live and none by the done date. Report the count and the oldest one monthly.

blocks.title: Measure adoption against the inventory
items: **Coverage is enforced divided by in scope.** Count both from the inventory weekly, by ring and business unit, and name the systems in the tail.
**MFA and passkeys.** In Entra, **Authentication methods** > **Activity** shows who is MFA or passwordless capable and how many sign-ins were single-factor; usage data needs P1 or P2[^authact].
**Conditional Access.** The gap analyzer workbook lists sign-ins no policy applied to, by user, app and location; it needs P1 and Log Analytics[^gap].

**EDR and ASR.** Compare onboarded with discovered devices in Defender's inventory[^discovery]. The ASR rules report needs Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 or Defender for Business; otherwise collect event 1122[^asrtest].

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Stopping at 80%.** The tail holds the old devices, service accounts, shared mailboxes and executives. Plan it as its own phase, with an owner per system.
**No owner after go-live.** Conditional Access policies have no owner field, so Microsoft suggests naming the owner in the policy name and keeping a register[^caplan]. Do that for every control.
**Piloting only in IT.** IT and lab devices often lack the business apps and drivers that break[^rings].
**Reporting deployed as done.** A policy left in audit mode looks finished on the status page and blocks nothing.

blocks.title: Security gates in IT and business projects
items: **At kickoff, ask six questions.** What data, who signs in and how, whether it faces the internet, which supplier or SaaS, who gets admin rights, and when it goes live.
**Rate the protection need: normal or high.** Grundschutz++ has only these two, and only high needs an explicit risk analysis[^std3001]. Rate it with the business owner in 30 minutes.

**Write the requirements into the plan.** Normal: a standard set, such as SSO with MFA, exportable logs, named admin roles, backups and patch deadlines. High: add a design review. For software you build, see the secure development sheet.

**Require a pentest before go-live** if the system faces the internet, has high need, is custom-built or changes how people sign in; ENISA expects tests at set-up and after significant upgrades[^enisatig]. Otherwise scan and check the configuration. For SaaS, test your tenant. Scope and providers: the penetration testing sheet.

**Sign off, then hand over.** Security confirms each requirement or lists what's open, with an owner and a date; management approves the risk of requirements not yet met[^std3001]. Name the operations owner and connect the logs.

blocks.title: Security in tenders and contracts
items: **Use the six NIS2 purchasing points.** Security requirements, updates for the whole lifetime or replacement after support ends, component information, security functions and secure configuration, assurance of compliance, and how you validate it[^enisatig]. They bind digital providers under Regulation 2024/2690; use them as everyone else's checklist.
**Ask when support ends.** From 11 December 2027, the CRA requires manufacturers to state the month and year at the time of purchase, and five years is a floor, not a default[^craguide].
**Require free, prompt fixes.** ENISA advises tenders that require tested fixes free of charge as soon as a security issue is known[^enisatig].
**Tie acceptance to evidence.** Make acceptance and the final payment depend on SSO and MFA working, logs flowing and critical pentest findings fixed. Add the third-party risk sheet's clauses.

blocks.title: Don't become the bottleneck
items: **Publish when security joins.** Grundschutz++ doesn't require the ISB to take an active role in every security-relevant project[^std3001]. Join high-need ones; normal ones use the checklist.
**Promise a turnaround,** such as 5 working days, as in the operating model sheet's service catalog. If security misses it, the project goes ahead and records the open items.
**Pre-approve patterns.** A standard SaaS requirement set, a contract annex and a reference design answer most questions in advance.
**Put a champion in the PMO** to ask the kickoff questions and call security in when a project rates high.

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **A risk analysis for every project.** Grundschutz++ needs none for normal protection need, because its requirements already build one in[^std3001].
**A pentest before every go-live.** A standard SaaS app behind SSO needs a configuration check.
**Auditing the standard ASR rules.** Microsoft says they can go to block or warn without testing[^asrplan].
**Months in report-only.** A week to a month of real sign-ins shows the impact. Enforce, then fix the tail.

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **Intune stages policy rollouts.** Deployment plans, in public preview since September 2026[^intunenew], push endpoint security and settings catalog policies to Windows ring by ring and can be paused or canceled[^intune].

**Conditional Access can stage itself with Microsoft 365 E5.** E5 now includes Security Copilot[^sccinc], whose Optimization Agent enforces a report-only policy in five phases and pauses if more than 10% of sign-ins are blocked[^caagent].
**Grundschutz++ asks you to write the project rule.** BSI-Standard 300-1 of 20 October 2026 requires a security role in security-relevant projects and a rule for when it takes part[^std3001].
**German NIS2 entities must secure their purchasing.** BSIG § 30 covers security in acquisition[^bsig30] and has applied since 6 December 2025, with no general transition period[^bsifaq].

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: The IT lead or provider runs rollouts; the managing director approves exceptions.
Pilot with two or three willing users, then everyone. Conditional Access templates start in report-only[^caplan].
Check IT purchases against the six NIS2 points.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Write one page per rollout: scope, target, rings, rollback trigger, exception rule, owner.
Report coverage weekly to the program's steering meeting.
Ask the kickoff questions in every IT project.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Ring by region or site, and hold mission-critical devices until the broad ring is done[^rings].
Make security sign-off a gate in the project method.
Put a security annex in every IT tender template.
